title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 49
paragraphs: However, Aristagoras the tyrant of Miletus arrived at Sparta while Cleomenes was reigning, and so it was with him that he came to speech. The Lacedaemonians say that he had with him a bronze tablet engraved with a map of the whole earth, with all the sea and all the rivers. When he came to speech with Cleomenes he said: “Do not marvel, Cleomenes, at my earnestness in coming here; for the case is this. That the sons of the Ionians should be slaves instead of free is a reproach and a grief most of all indeed to ourselves, but to you above all others, inasmuch as you are the leaders of Hellas. Now therefore I entreat you by the gods of Hellas to rescue from slavery the Ionians, who are your own kinsmen. You may easily achieve this, for the barbarians are not brave in battle, whereas you have reached the very height of valor in matters of war; and their fighting is of this sort—with bows and a short spear, and they go into battle wearing trousers and caps on their heads. So they are easily conquered. Then again, those who occupy that continent have good things in such quantities as all the other nations of the world put together do not possess: first gold, then silver and bronze, embroidered garments, beasts of burden, and slaves—all of which you could have for yourselves if you so desired. The nations moreover are arranged one after another as I shall show: the Ionians here; next to them the Lydians, who not only live in a fertile land but are also exceedingly rich in gold and silver,”—as he said this he pointed to the map of the earth he carried with him engraved on the tablet—“and here next to the Lydians,” Aristagoras went on, “are the Eastern Phrygians, who have the greatest number of sheep and cattle of any people I know, and also the most abundant crops. Next to the Phrygians are the Cappadocians, whom we call Syrians; and bordering them are the Cilicians, coming down to this sea, in which lies the island of Cyprus here; and these pay five hundred talents to the king as their yearly tribute. Next to these Cilicians are the Armenians, whom you see here, and these too have great numbers of sheep and cattle. Next to the Armenians are the Matieni, occupying this country here; and next to them is the land of Cissia here, in which, along the banks of this river Choaspes, is situated the city of Susa, where the Great King has his residence and where the money is laid up in treasuries. Once you have taken this city, you may then confidently enter into a contest with Zeus himself in the matter of wealth. No—can it really be that you feel obliged to take on the risk of battles against the Messenians and Arcadians and Argives, who are a match for you, for the sake of land that is not much in extent nor very fertile, and for boundaries that are merely small, though these peoples have no gold or silver at all, which are what makes a man eager to fight and die? Can this be so? Will you not now choose another course, when it is possible for you easily to have rule over all Asia?” So Aristagoras spoke, and Cleomenes answered him: “Milesian guest-friend, I defer my answer to you until the day after tomorrow.”
